title: Saul Rejected After the Amalekite War
overview: King Saul is ordered to wipe out the Amalekites, keeps their king and best animals instead, and is told that God has rejected him as king.

parts.label: The order against Amalek (vv. 1-3)
parts.note: Samuel tells Saul to attack the Amalekites, a desert people who had attacked Israel's weakest stragglers after the escape from Egypt (Exodus 17, Deuteronomy 25). The order is to kill every person and animal, children and infants included, 'devoting' everything to God by destroying it so no one could keep any of it as loot.

parts.label: The attack and the Kenites (vv. 4-9)
parts.note: Saul warns the Kenites, relatives of Moses' father-in-law who had helped Israel in the wilderness, to leave before he attacks. His army kills the Amalekite people but keeps King Agag alive along with the best animals, destroying only what was weak or worthless.

parts.label: Caught out by the animals (vv. 10-21)
parts.note: The LORD tells Samuel he regrets making Saul king, and Samuel is angry and cries out to God all night. Saul, fresh from setting up a monument to himself, claims he obeyed, but the noise of the captured animals gives him away, so he blames his soldiers and says the animals are for sacrifice.

parts.label: Listening over offerings (vv. 22-31)
parts.note: Samuel answers in poetry that God values listening to him more than animal offerings, and that because Saul rejected God's word, God rejects him as king. When Saul, now admitting he feared his men, grabs Samuel's robe and it tears, Samuel calls it a sign that the kingdom is torn from Saul and given to someone better, soon revealed as David.

parts.label: Agag is killed (vv. 32-33)
parts.note: Agag expects to be spared, and the translations differ on whether he comes in chains or cheerfully, because the Hebrew word is unclear. Samuel says that as Agag's sword left mothers childless, so will his mother be, and he puts Agag to death before the LORD at Gilgal (some translations say he cut him to pieces).

parts.label: Samuel and Saul part (vv. 34-35)
parts.note: Samuel goes home and never visits Saul again, yet he grieves for him. The chapter repeats that the LORD regretted making Saul king, even though verse 29 says God does not change his mind like a human, and readers have long puzzled over how these fit together.

disagreement: Many readers find the order to kill every Amalekite, infants included, deeply troubling, and Christians differ on how to read it. Some see it as God's just judgment in a unique moment of history. Others read it as exaggerated ancient war language, or as the writers' limited picture of God, which they read in light of Jesus' teaching. Many early Christian teachers read Amalek as a picture of the sin a believer must fight. Jewish readers have long wrestled with this passage too.
think: Saul says he gave in because he was afraid of his own men; where have you seen fear of other people's opinion quietly steer a decision?
